newsitem.title: UK: Channel ferry merger targets debt, tunnel problems.
newsitem.headline: Channel ferry merger targets debt, tunnel problems.

text.p: The planned merger of P&O and Stena Line's English Channel ferry businesses is meant to attack the problems of high financing costs and competition with Eurotunnel's channel tunnel, the firms said on Thursday.

P&O, the Peninsular & Oriental Steam Navigation Company, said a new jointly-held ferry company would absorb 173 million stg of its group borrowings and other liabilites and in return it would receive 60 percent of the ordinary shares and 51 million stg of cumulative redeemable preference shares.
Stena will transfer assets and businesses in return for 134 million stg in cash, plus 40 percent of the shares.
The P&O assets have an estimated book value of either 225 or 280 million stg as at the end of 1996, while the Stena assets were estimated to be worth 185 million stg.

The two figures came from parallel statements, which also differed over the impact of the asset sale on Stena's debt. One said it would cut it by 120 million stg, the other 134 million. "As a result of improved profits due to (envisaged) cost savings, high depreciation and low capital commitments, the new company will have strongly positive cash flow. Since borrowings are therefore likely to fall rapidly a high level of initial gearing is appropriate," the firms added.
On market share, the two presented a calculation of their view of how they would have competed with Eurotunnel between Dover and Calais during August this year.

According to the partners, they would have held 41 percent of the market for cars, equal to Eurotunnel's share, while they would have had 40 percent of the freight market compared with Eurotunnel's 44 percent.

Other lines, mainly French state railways-owned Sea France, Hoverspeed (owned by Sea Containers ) and newly-merged Finnish-Australian Holyman Sally, have 18 percent of the car market and 16 percent of the freight.
